title: Complete SQL Learning Roadmap: From Beginner to Advanced Architect
content:
A comprehensive 4-stage pedagogical roadmap for mastering SQL:

1) Stage 1 — Fundamentals (Syntax & Foundations):
- Relational data model: Tables, rows, columns, data types, constraints (PK, FK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK).
- Basic querying: SELECT, projection, arithmetic, DISTINCT, column/table aliasing (AS).
- Filtering: WHERE clause with comparison operators (=, !=, <, >, <=, >=), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT), IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.
- Sorting & Limiting: ORDER BY (ASC/DESC, NULLS FIRST/LAST), LIMIT, OFFSET, TOP, FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY.

2) Stage 2 — Intermediate (Data Analysis & Manipulation):
- Relational Joins: INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN, CROSS JOIN, Self Joins, Anti-Joins.
- Grouping & Aggregations: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, GROUP BY, HAVING clause, conditional aggregation.
- Subqueries: Scalar subqueries, multi-row subqueries (IN, ANY, ALL), correlated subqueries (EXISTS / NOT EXISTS).
- Set Theory: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT / MINUS.
- Conditional Logic: Simple and Searched CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END expressions, COALESCE, NULLIF.
- DDL & DML: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE.

3) Stage 3 — Advanced (Analytical Engineering & Complex Logic):
- Window Functions: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), NTILE(), LAG(), LEAD(), FIRST_VALUE(), LAST_VALUE().
- Window Framing: ROWS vs RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
- Common Table Expressions (CTEs): Non-recursive CTEs and Recursive CTEs (Hierarchical trees, Gaps & Islands).
- Semi-structured data: JSON extraction, parsing JSON arrays, XML manipulation.
- Date & Time mastery: DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT, INTERVAL arithmetic, timezone handling.

4) Stage 4 — Database Internals & Performance Tuning (Senior / Architect):
- Indexing internals: B-Tree, Hash, GIN, GiST, BRIN, Covering indexes (INCLUDE), Partial/Filtered indexes.
- Query optimization: EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution plans, SARGable queries, eliminating sequential scans.
- Concurrency & Transactions: ACID properties, Isolation levels (Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable), MVCC, WAL, Deadlock prevention.
- Database Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, Star & Snowflake schemas.
- Stored Procedures, UDFs, Triggers, Views, and Materialized Views.

title: SQL Practice Topics: Core Skills to Build Hands-On Mastery
tags: topic of sql to start practice
content:
High-yield SQL topics to practice systematically for interviews and production data projects:

1) Multi-Table Join Scenarios:
- Joining 3+ tables with business conditions.
- Anti-joins: Finding rows in Table A with no matching rows in Table B using LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL vs NOT EXISTS.
- Self-joins: Finding employees with their direct managers or finding overlapping date ranges.

2) Aggregation with Complex Grouping:
- Finding top N categories by sales volume using HAVING.
- Pivoting data using conditional aggregation: SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 'Q1' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END).
- Advanced aggregation: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE for multi-dimensional sub-totals.

3) Advanced Analytical Window Queries:
- Top 3 highest-earning employees in each department using DENSE_RANK().
- Month-over-Month (MoM) revenue growth: ((rev - LAG(rev)) / LAG(rev)) * 100.
- Running cumulative totals and 7-day rolling moving averages.

4) Recursive CTEs & Graph Traversal:
- Building organization hierarchy paths: Employee -> Manager -> VP -> CEO.
- Generating continuous number or date sequences to identify missing dates (Gaps & Islands).

5) Performance & Indexing Scenarios:
- Rewriting non-SARGable queries (e.g. `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024` -> `WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01'`).
- Evaluating query plans with EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify sequential scans vs index seeks.

title: SQL Technical Interview Cheatsheet: Rapid Concept Review
content:
Key SQL interview concepts and their core definitions:

1) Query Execution Order:
FROM -> ON -> JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT / OFFSET.

2) WHERE vs HAVING:
WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation; HAVING filters aggregated groups after GROUP BY.

3) UNION vs UNION ALL:
UNION removes duplicates by performing an internal distinct sort; UNION ALL simply appends results and is much faster.

4) DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP:
- DELETE: DML statement, row-by-row deletion, fully logged, triggers fire, can be rolled back.
- TRUNCATE: DDL statement, deallocates data pages, resets auto-increment IDs, minimal logging, faster, no triggers.
- DROP: DDL statement, completely removes the table definition, data, and indexes from database catalog.

5) Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index:
- Clustered: Defines physical ordering of rows in the data pages (only 1 per table).
- Non-Clustered: Separate B-Tree structure storing index keys with pointers (row IDs) to the data rows.

6) Primary Key vs Unique Key:
- Primary Key: Uniquely identifies each row, cannot contain NULLs, only one PK per table.
- Unique Key: Enforces uniqueness across rows, allows one (or multiple depending on dialect) NULL value.

title: Logical SQL Query Execution Order Explained
content:
Relational database engines process SQL clauses in a strict logical order that differs from written syntax:

1) FROM: Database identifies source tables and executes Cartesian products.
2) ON: Evaluates join conditions between tables.
3) JOIN: Performs table joins (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER, CROSS).
4) WHERE: Filters base rows matching Boolean filter predicates.
5) GROUP BY: Collapses remaining rows into aggregated buckets by group keys.
6) HAVING: Filters aggregated buckets based on aggregate function conditions.
7) SELECT: Evaluates expressions, column projections, and window functions.
8) DISTINCT: Eliminates duplicate row projections across selected columns.
9) ORDER BY: Sorts the final result set by specified columns or expressions.
10) LIMIT / OFFSET (FETCH): Applies pagination and caps the number of output rows.

Why This Matters:
- You cannot use a column alias defined in SELECT inside the WHERE clause because WHERE executes before SELECT.
- You can use column aliases in ORDER BY because ORDER BY executes after SELECT.

title: WHERE vs HAVING Clause: Detailed Comparison & Architectural Differences
content:
Comparison of WHERE and HAVING clauses in relational SQL:

1) Execution Timing:
- WHERE executes BEFORE grouping and aggregation. It filters base table rows.
- HAVING executes AFTER the GROUP BY phase. It filters aggregated group records.

2) Aggregation Functions:
- WHERE cannot contain aggregate functions like `SUM()`, `AVG()`, `COUNT()`. (e.g. `WHERE COUNT(*) > 5` causes a syntax error).
- HAVING is specifically designed to filter on aggregate functions (e.g. `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`).

3) Index Usage:
- WHERE can utilize B-Tree indexes on filtered columns to avoid full table scans.
- HAVING operates on computed aggregate buffers in memory/tempdb after grouping.

```sql
-- Correct Usage:
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM employees
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'                -- Row-level filter (WHERE)
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > 75000;            -- Aggregate filter (HAVING)
```

title: LIMIT, OFFSET, TOP, and FETCH FIRST: Dialect Differences & Pagination
content:
Methods to restrict output row counts and paginate results across SQL dialects:

1) PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite:
```sql
SELECT emp_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;
```

2) Microsoft SQL Server (T-SQL):
```sql
-- Legacy Top
SELECT TOP 10 emp_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;

-- ANSI SQL:2008 Standard in modern T-SQL
SELECT emp_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC
OFFSET 20 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY;
```

3) Oracle Database:
```sql
SELECT emp_name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC
FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;
```

Performance Note on Deep Pagination:
Using `OFFSET 1000000` forces the database engine to read and discard 1 million rows. For massive tables, use **Keyset Pagination (Seek Method)**:
```sql
SELECT id, emp_name, salary FROM employees
WHERE id > :last_seen_id
ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 10;
```

title: QUALIFY Clause: Filtering Window Function Results Directly
content:
The QUALIFY clause filters results of Window Functions directly without requiring an intermediate CTE or subquery:

Supported Dialects: Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Databricks SQL, Teradata, DuckDB.

Standard SQL without QUALIFY (requires Subquery or CTE):
```sql
WITH RankedEmployees AS (
    SELECT emp_name, department_id, salary,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) as rnk
    FROM employees
)
SELECT * FROM RankedEmployees WHERE rnk = 1;
```

With QUALIFY (Clean & Direct):
```sql
SELECT emp_name, department_id, salary
FROM employees
QUALIFY DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1;
```

title: Master Guide to Relational Joins: Mechanics, Types, and Venn Diagrams
content:
Relational joins combine columns from one or more tables based on related keys:

1) INNER JOIN: Returns rows when there is a match in BOTH tables.
2) LEFT (OUTER) JOIN: Returns all rows from left table, with matching rows from right table (or NULL if no match).
3) RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN: Returns all rows from right table, with matching rows from left table (or NULL if no match).
4) FULL (OUTER) JOIN: Returns all rows when there is a match in either table (combines LEFT and RIGHT).
5) CROSS JOIN: Produces a Cartesian product (every row in table A paired with every row in table B; $M \times N$ rows).
6) SELF JOIN: Joins a table to itself to compare rows within the same relation (e.g. employee-to-manager hierarchy).
7) ANTI-JOIN: Returns rows from left table where NO matching row exists in right table (`LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL`).
8) SEMI-JOIN: Returns rows from left table that match at least one row in right table without duplicating left rows (`WHERE EXISTS (...)`).

title: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN: Behavioral Differences & Nullability
tags: difference between inner and left join
when to use inner vs left join
content:
Comparison of INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN:

1) INNER JOIN:
- Returns ONLY rows where the join predicate evaluates to TRUE in both tables.
- Discards unmatched rows from both sides.
- Use when related foreign key data is strictly required.

```sql
-- Returns only employees assigned to an active department
SELECT e.emp_name, d.department_name
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
```

2) LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN):
- Preserves ALL rows from the left table regardless of whether a match exists in the right table.
- Populates right table columns with `NULL` when no match is found.
- Use when keeping parent/primary records is mandatory even if child/optional records are missing.

```sql
-- Returns ALL employees, showing NULL for those without a department
SELECT e.emp_name, COALESCE(d.department_name, 'Unassigned') AS department_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
```

title: Anti-Joins and Semi-Joins: Patterns, Syntax, and Optimization
tags: not exists vs left join null
content:
Anti-Joins and Semi-Joins are core relational patterns for set matching:

1) Anti-Join (Find records in A that have NO match in B):
- Approach 1: `NOT EXISTS` (Recommended for performance and NULL safety):
```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
);
```
- Approach 2: `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL`:
```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
```

2) Semi-Join (Find records in A that have AT LEAST ONE match in B, without multiplying rows):
- Using `EXISTS`:
```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.total_amount > 1000
);
```
Note: An `INNER JOIN` might duplicate customer rows if a customer has multiple orders > $1000. `EXISTS` prevents row duplication.

title: LATERAL Joins and CROSS APPLY: Row-by-Row Correlated Joins
content:
LATERAL joins (PostgreSQL, MySQL 8.0.14+, Oracle) and CROSS APPLY (SQL Server, Oracle) allow subqueries in the FROM clause to reference columns from preceding tables:

1) Problem Solved: Standard joins cannot pass a column from the left table into a subquery inside the join clause.

2) PostgreSQL / MySQL / Oracle syntax (`CROSS JOIN LATERAL`):
```sql
-- For each customer, get their top 2 most recent orders
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.total_amount
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT order_id, order_date, total_amount
    FROM orders
    WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id
    ORDER BY order_date DESC
    LIMIT 2
) o;
```

3) SQL Server T-SQL syntax (`CROSS APPLY`):
```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.total_amount
FROM customers c
CROSS APPLY (
    SELECT TOP 2 order_id, order_date, total_amount
    FROM orders
    WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id
    ORDER BY order_date DESC
) o;
```
Note: Use `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON TRUE` or `OUTER APPLY` to preserve customers who have 0 orders.

title: Mastering SQL Window Functions: OVER, PARTITION BY, and ORDER BY
content:
Window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows related to the current row without collapsing them into a single row (unlike GROUP BY):

Core Syntax Structure:
```sql
FUNCTION() OVER (
    PARTITION BY partition_column
    ORDER BY sort_column ASC/DESC
    ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN frame_start AND frame_end
)
```

Key Components:
1) `PARTITION BY`: Divides rows into logical groups/windows (like GROUP BY, but preserves individual row granularity).
2) `ORDER BY`: Defines the logical sort order within each partition.
3) Frame Specification (`ROWS` or `RANGE`): Determines the exact subset of rows included in the window calculation relative to current row.

title: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK: Comprehensive Comparison
tags: give me sql query to get row number
content:
Comparison of ranking window functions when handling tie values (e.g. salaries: [1000, 900, 900, 800]):

1) `ROW_NUMBER()`:
- Assigns a unique sequential integer to every row regardless of duplicate values.
- Ties are broken arbitrarily (unless additional ORDER BY tie-breakers are provided).
- Output: `1, 2, 3, 4`

2) `RANK()`:
- Assigns the same rank to duplicate values, but SKIPS subsequent ranks to preserve absolute rank counts.
- Output: `1, 2, 2, 4` (Notice rank 3 is skipped).

3) `DENSE_RANK()`:
- Assigns the same rank to duplicate values WITHOUT skipping numbers.
- Output: `1, 2, 2, 3` (Dense sequence).

```sql
SELECT emp_name, department_id, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) as row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) as rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) as dense_rnk
FROM employees;
```

title: NTILE Function: Bucket Distribution, Quartiles, and Deciles
content:
The `NTILE(n)` window function divides ordered rows in a partition into `n` approximately equal-sized buckets/groups:

How it Works:
- Assigns a bucket number from 1 to `n` to each row.
- If the total row count is not evenly divisible by `n`, the extra rows are distributed starting from bucket 1 downwards.

Common Use Cases:
- Quartiles: `NTILE(4)` (Top 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%).
- Deciles: `NTILE(10)` (Customer segmentation).
- Median splitting: `NTILE(2)`.

```sql
-- Segment customers into 4 spending quartiles
SELECT customer_id, total_spend,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS spending_quartile
FROM customer_analytics;
```

title: LAG and LEAD: Time Series, Offsets, and Period-over-Period Calculations
content:
`LAG()` and `LEAD()` access values from previous or following rows within a partition without needing a self-join:

Syntax:
`LAG(column, offset, default_value) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)`

1) `LAG(val, 1, 0)`: Accesses the value of `val` from 1 row before current row.
2) `LEAD(val, 1, 0)`: Accesses the value of `val` from 1 row after current row.

```sql
-- Calculate Month-over-Month Revenue Growth
SELECT
    sales_month,
    revenue,
    LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sales_month) AS prev_month_revenue,
    ROUND(((revenue - LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sales_month)) /
           LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY sales_month)) * 100.0, 2) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM monthly_sales;
```

title: Window Framing: ROWS vs RANGE BETWEEN Specification
content:
Window framing specifies the exact boundaries of rows evaluated by aggregate window functions:

1) `ROWS BETWEEN`:
- Evaluates physical row counts.
- `ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`: Current row + previous 2 physical rows (3-row rolling moving average).
- `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`: Running cumulative total from the start of the partition.

2) `RANGE BETWEEN`:
- Evaluates logical value boundaries (treats rows with duplicate ORDER BY keys identically).
- Default behavior if frame is omitted with ORDER BY: `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` (Watch out: Duplicate values will sum together simultaneously!).

```sql
-- 7-Day Moving Average of Sales
SELECT sale_date, daily_amount,
       AVG(daily_amount) OVER (
           ORDER BY sale_date
           ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS moving_avg_7d
FROM daily_revenue;
```

title: Common Table Expressions (CTEs): WITH Clause, Syntax, and Readability
tags: what is cte and how to write cte query
content:
A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a temporary named result set defined within the execution scope of a single `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` statement:

Syntax:
```sql
WITH HighValueCustomers AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(order_total) AS lifetime_value
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING SUM(order_total) >= 10000
),
CustomerRegions AS (
    SELECT customer_id, region, country
    FROM customers
)
SELECT h.customer_id, r.region, h.lifetime_value
FROM HighValueCustomers h
JOIN CustomerRegions r ON h.customer_id = r.customer_id
ORDER BY h.lifetime_value DESC;
```

Advantages over Subqueries:
1) Readability: Organizes query logic sequentially from top to bottom.
2) Reusability: A single CTE can be referenced multiple times within the same query.
3) Recursion: Supports recursive queries for hierarchical tree graphs.

title: Recursive CTEs: Traversing Hierarchies, Org Charts, and Graphs
content:
Recursive CTEs repeatedly execute an initial query (anchor member) and union it with a recursive query (recursive member) until no new rows are returned:

Standard 3-Part Structure:
1) **Anchor Member**: Base query returning top-level nodes (e.g. CEO where `manager_id IS NULL`).
2) **UNION ALL**: Combines anchor and recursive steps.
3) **Recursive Member**: Joins the CTE back to the base table to fetch next child levels, with a termination condition.

```sql
-- Traversal of Employee-to-Manager Organizational Hierarchy
WITH RECURSIVE OrgHierarchy AS (
    -- 1. Anchor: Top-level executives
    SELECT emp_id, emp_name, manager_id, 1 AS level, CAST(emp_name AS VARCHAR(1000)) AS path
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- 2. Recursive: Subordinates
    SELECT e.emp_id, e.emp_name, e.manager_id, o.level + 1, CAST(o.path || ' -> ' || e.emp_name AS VARCHAR(1000))
    FROM employees e
    INNER JOIN OrgHierarchy o ON e.manager_id = o.emp_id
)
SELECT emp_id, emp_name, level, path
FROM OrgHierarchy
ORDER BY level, emp_id;
```

title: Gaps and Islands Problem: Identification and Solution Patterns
content:
The 'Gaps and Islands' problem is a classic SQL challenge involving consecutive sequence analysis:
- **Islands**: Contiguous ranges of consecutive numbers or dates (e.g. customer login streaks).
- **Gaps**: Missing ranges between sequences.

The Difference-of-Row-Numbers Pattern (DENSE_RANK Technique):
Subtracting a sequential row number (`ROW_NUMBER()`) from a sequential sequence value yields a **constant group identifier** for contiguous rows!

```sql
-- Find consecutive login streaks for users
WITH NumberedLogins AS (
    SELECT user_id, login_date,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS rn,
           login_date - CAST(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS INT) AS island_group
    FROM (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM user_logins) t
)
SELECT user_id,
       MIN(login_date) AS streak_start,
       MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
       COUNT(*) AS streak_length_days
FROM NumberedLogins
GROUP BY user_id, island_group
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
```

title: PIVOT and UNPIVOT: Transforming Rows to Columns and Columns to Rows
content:
Transforming relational rows into columns (pivoting) and columns into rows (unpivoting):

1) Cross-Dialect Pivoting via Conditional Aggregation (Standard SQL):
```sql
SELECT
    department_id,
    SUM(CASE WHEN job_title = 'Engineer' THEN salary ELSE 0 END) AS engineer_salary,
    SUM(CASE WHEN job_title = 'Manager'  THEN salary ELSE 0 END) AS manager_salary,
    SUM(CASE WHEN job_title = 'Analyst'  THEN salary ELSE 0 END) AS analyst_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id;
```

2) Native PIVOT clause (SQL Server / Oracle / Snowflake):
```sql
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT department_id, job_title, salary FROM employees
) src
PIVOT (
    SUM(salary) FOR job_title IN ([Engineer], [Manager], [Analyst])
) pvt;
```

3) UNPIVOT / CROSS JOIN LATERAL (Columns to Rows):
```sql
SELECT department_id, job_title, salary
FROM employee_summary
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    VALUES ('Engineer', engineer_salary), ('Manager', manager_salary)
) AS v(job_title, salary);
```

title: Top N Records Per Group: Patterns, Tradeoffs, and Window Ranking
tags: sql query to get top 5 highest salaried employee
content:
How to retrieve the top $N$ records within each category/group efficiently:

Recommended Pattern (using `DENSE_RANK()` inside a CTE):
```sql
WITH RankedEmployees AS (
    SELECT emp_id, emp_name, department_id, salary,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY department_id
               ORDER BY salary DESC
           ) AS rank_in_dept
    FROM employees
)
SELECT emp_id, emp_name, department_id, salary, rank_in_dept
FROM RankedEmployees
WHERE rank_in_dept <= 3
ORDER BY department_id, rank_in_dept;
```

Why NOT `LIMIT` in subquery:
Standard `LIMIT` restricts total output across the whole table, not per partition. Window functions partition and rank independently per group.

title: SARGable Predicates: Writing High-Performance Index-Friendly WHERE Clauses
content:
A SARGable query (Search Argument Able) is formatted so the Cost-Based Optimizer can utilize index seek operations rather than performing a full table scan:

Non-SARGable Anti-Patterns vs SARGable Corrections:

1) Date Functions wrapping indexed columns:
- ❌ Non-SARGable: `WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024`
- ✅ SARGable: `WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01'`

2) String Wildcard Prefix:
- ❌ Non-SARGable: `WHERE customer_name LIKE '%Smith'` (forces full scan)
- ✅ SARGable: `WHERE customer_name LIKE 'Smith%'` (uses B-Tree index prefix seek)

3) Mathematical functions on columns:
- ❌ Non-SARGable: `WHERE salary * 1.10 > 50000`
- ✅ SARGable: `WHERE salary > 50000 / 1.10`

4) String Concatenation:
- ❌ Non-SARGable: `WHERE first_name || ' ' || last_name = 'John Doe'`
- ✅ SARGable: `WHERE first_name = 'John' AND last_name = 'Doe'`

title: Database Index Architecture: B-Tree, Hash, Clustered, and Covering Indexes
content:
Overview of relational database index types and physical structures:

1) B-Tree Index (Balanced Tree):
- Default general-purpose index in almost all RDBMS (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server).
- Supports equality (`=`), range queries (`<, <=, >, >=, BETWEEN`), sorting (`ORDER BY`), and prefix matching (`LIKE 'ABC%'`).
- Time complexity: $O(\log N)$.

2) Clustered Index vs Non-Clustered Index:
- **Clustered Index**: The leaf level IS the actual data page. Table rows are physically stored on disk in the index sort order. Only 1 clustered index can exist per table.
- **Non-Clustered Index**: Separate B-tree where leaf nodes contain pointers (Row IDs or Clustered Key) to the data page.

3) Covering Index (`INCLUDE` Clause):
- Contains all columns referenced in the query (SELECT, WHERE, JOIN), enabling an **Index-Only Scan** without touching base table pages (eliminates heap lookup/bookmark lookup).
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_covering ON orders (customer_id, status) INCLUDE (total_amount, order_date);
```

4) Composite Index (Multi-Column) & Left-to-Right Rule:
- An index on `(A, B, C)` can serve queries on `(A)`, `(A, B)`, and `(A, B, C)`, but CANNOT serve queries on `(B)` or `(C)` alone.

title: Internal Join Algorithms: Nested Loop, Hash Join, and Merge Join
content:
How database query engines execute joins internally under the hood:

1) Nested Loop Join:
- For each outer row, the engine scans/seeks the inner table.
- Best when outer table is small and inner table has a fast index on join column.
- Time complexity: $O(M \times \log N)$ with index.

2) Hash Join:
- Builds an in-memory hash table on the smaller table, then streams the larger table to probe hash matches.
- Best for large unindexed datasets with equality join predicates (`ON a.id = b.id`).
- High memory usage; spills to disk (tempdb) if hash table exceeds `work_mem`.

3) Merge Join (Sort-Merge Join):
- Both inputs must be pre-sorted on join key. Scans both inputs in lockstep like a zipper.
- Optimal for massive pre-sorted or indexed datasets.

title: ACID Properties in Relational Databases Explained
content:
The 4 pillars of database transaction reliability (ACID):

1) **Atomicity (All or Nothing)**:
- Every SQL statement in a transaction is treated as a single indivisible unit. If any statement fails, the entire transaction rolls back (`ROLLBACK`).

2) **Consistency (Rules & Invariants Preserved)**:
- Database transitions strictly from one valid state to another, upholding all constraints (PK, FK, CHECK, triggers).

3) **Isolation (Concurrent Independence)**:
- Concurrent transactions execute without interfering with one another's intermediate states (governed by Isolation Levels).

4) **Durability (Committed Changes Persist)**:
- Once a transaction commits (`COMMIT`), its data updates survive system crashes and power failures via Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and disk flush.

title: Transaction Isolation Levels: Phenomena, Dirty Reads, and Serialization
content:
ANSI SQL Transaction Isolation Levels and concurrency phenomena:

Phenomena:
- **Dirty Read**: Reading uncommitted changes made by another transaction.
- **Non-Repeatable Read**: Re-reading the same row within a transaction returns altered values because another transaction committed an update.
- **Phantom Read**: Re-running a range query returns newly inserted/deleted rows committed by another transaction.

Isolation Level Matrix:
| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Non-Repeatable Read | Phantom Read |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Read Uncommitted** | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| **Read Committed** (Default in PG/Oracle/SQL Server) | ❌ Prevented | Possible | Possible |
| **Repeatable Read** (Default in MySQL InnoDB) | ❌ Prevented | ❌ Prevented | Possible (or MVCC prevented) |
| **Serializable** (Highest Isolation) | ❌ Prevented | ❌ Prevented | ❌ Prevented |

```sql
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
-- Queries execute with snapshot consistency
COMMIT;
```

title: MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) and Database Locks
content:
How modern database systems achieve high concurrency without blocking reads:

1) MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control):
- "Readers do not block writers, and writers do not block readers."
- Implemented in PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle, and SQL Server RCSI.
- Creates snapshot row versions with transaction IDs (`xmin`/`xmax`). A SELECT query reads the snapshot corresponding to its transaction start time.

2) Lock Types:
- **Shared Lock (S-Lock)**: Acquired for reading; multiple transactions can hold shared locks simultaneously.
- **Exclusive Lock (X-Lock)**: Acquired for writing/modifying (`UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `INSERT`); blocks all other readers and writers.
- **Intent Locks (IS, IX)**: Table-level markers indicating row-level lock intentions.

3) Deadlocks:
- Occurs when Transaction A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2, while Transaction B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1.
- The database deadlock detector automatically detects cyclic wait graphs and aborts one transaction as a victim.

title: Database Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF Explained with Examples
content:
Database Normalization organizes tables to reduce data redundancy and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies:

1) First Normal Form (1NF):
- Each column must contain atomic (indivisible) values.
- No repeating groups or arrays stored in a single cell.
- Every row must be uniquely identifiable with a primary key.

2) Second Normal Form (2NF):
- Must be in 1NF.
- Eliminate partial dependency: Every non-key attribute must depend on the WHOLE primary key (relevant when PK is composite).

3) Third Normal Form (3NF):
- Must be in 2NF.
- Eliminate transitive dependency: Non-key attributes must depend directly on the primary key, NOT on other non-key attributes ("Every attribute must depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key, so help me Codd").

4) Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF):
- Stricter version of 3NF.
- For every functional dependency $X \rightarrow Y$, $X$ must be a superkey.

title: Stored Procedures vs User-Defined Functions (UDF): Architectural Comparison
content:
Comprehensive comparison between Stored Procedures (SP) and User-Defined Functions (UDF):

1) Stored Procedure (SP):
- Executed via `CALL sp_name(params)` or `EXEC sp_name`.
- Can execute DML statements (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`), DDL, and control transactions (`COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`).
- Can return zero, one, or multiple result sets.
- CANNOT be called directly inside a `SELECT` query statement.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL Stored Procedure with Transaction Management
CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE transfer_funds(sender_id INT, receiver_id INT, amount NUMERIC)
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - amount WHERE account_id = sender_id;
    UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + amount WHERE account_id = receiver_id;
    COMMIT;
END;
$$;

-- Invocation:
CALL transfer_funds(101, 202, 500.00);
```

2) User-Defined Function (UDF):
- Executed inside SQL expressions (e.g. `SELECT fn_calculate_tax(salary) FROM employees`).
- Must return a single scalar value or a table (Table-Valued Function TVF).
- CANNOT execute transaction controls (`COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK`) or modify database state in analytical calls.

title: Standard Views vs Materialized Views: Storage, Performance, and Refresh
content:
Comparison of Standard Views and Materialized Views:

1) Standard View (Virtual Table):
- Does NOT store physical data on disk.
- Acts as a saved SQL query. Whenever queried, the database dynamically expands the view definition and executes the underlying SQL query.
- Always returns real-time data with zero storage overhead, but re-computes expensive joins on every call.

```sql
CREATE VIEW active_customer_orders AS
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, o.order_id, o.total_amount
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'COMPLETED';
```

2) Materialized View (Physically Persisted):
- Executes query once and stores the physical result set on disk as a table with its own indexes.
- Instant query response for complex analytical aggregations.
- Data can become stale until refreshed (`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY view_name;`).

title: SQL Dialect Matrix: String Concatenation and Substring Across Databases
tags: concat in postgres mysql oracle sqlserver
content:
String manipulation syntax across the top relational database engines:

1) String Concatenation:
- **PostgreSQL / Oracle / SQLite**: `first_name || ' ' || last_name`
- **MySQL**: `CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)`
- **SQL Server (T-SQL)**: `first_name + ' ' + last_name` or `CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)`

2) String Length:
- **PostgreSQL / MySQL / Oracle**: `LENGTH(col)` or `CHAR_LENGTH(col)`
- **SQL Server**: `LEN(col)`

3) Substrings:
- **PostgreSQL / MySQL / Oracle / SQLite**: `SUBSTRING(col FROM 1 FOR 5)` or `SUBSTR(col, 1, 5)`
- **SQL Server**: `SUBSTRING(col, 1, 5)`

title: SQL Dialect Matrix: Date & Time Manipulation Across Databases
tags: postgres date vs sql server date
content:
Date and time arithmetic syntax across database platforms:

1) Current Timestamp:
- **ANSI SQL / PostgreSQL**: `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` or `NOW()`
- **MySQL**: `NOW()` or `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`
- **SQL Server**: `GETDATE()` or `SYSDATETIME()`
- **Oracle**: `SYSDATE` or `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`
- **SQLite**: `datetime('now')`

2) Date Truncation (e.g. Month Start):
- **PostgreSQL**: `DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)`
- **MySQL**: `DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m-01')`
- **SQL Server**: `DATETRUNC(month, order_date)` or `DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(d), MONTH(d), 1)`
- **Oracle**: `TRUNC(order_date, 'MM')`

3) Date Difference:
- **PostgreSQL**: `end_date - start_date` (returns integer days) or `AGE(end_date, start_date)`
- **SQL Server**: `DATEDIFF(day, start_date, end_date)`
- **MySQL**: `DATEDIFF(end_date, start_date)`

title: SQL Sub-Languages Explained: DDL, DML, DQL, TCL, and DCL
content:
Relational SQL commands are divided into 5 standardized sub-languages:

1) **DQL (Data Query Language)**:
- Commands used to retrieve data from tables: `SELECT`.

2) **DML (Data Manipulation Language)**:
- Commands that modify data records (row-level changes): `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `MERGE`.

3) **DDL (Data Definition Language)**:
- Commands that define and modify schema objects: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `RENAME`.
- Implicitly commits active transactions in most systems.

4) **TCL (Transaction Control Language)**:
- Commands that manage transactional integrity: `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`.

5) **DCL (Data Control Language)**:
- Commands that manage security and access permissions: `GRANT`, `REVOKE`.

title: Complete SQL Learning Roadmap & Step-by-Step Study Guide
content:
A structured step-by-step roadmap to master SQL from absolute beginner to senior database engineer:

1) Phase 1 — SQL Fundamentals (Beginner):
- Relational concepts: Tables, Rows, Columns, Primary Keys, Foreign Keys.
- Basic queries: SELECT, DISTINCT, WHERE, AND/OR/NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL.
- Sorting & Limiting: ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET, TOP.
- Basic calculations: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.

2) Phase 2 — Intermediate SQL (Data Analysis & Manipulation):
- Table Joins: INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN, CROSS JOIN, Self Joins.
- Aggregations: GROUP BY, HAVING clause, COUNT(DISTINCT).
- Subqueries: Scalar subqueries, multi-row subqueries (IN, ANY, ALL), correlated subqueries (EXISTS).
- Set Operations: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT.
- Conditional logic: CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END.
- DDL & DML: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE.

3) Phase 3 — Advanced SQL (Analytics & Data Engineering):
- Window Functions: ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), NTILE(), LAG(), LEAD(), Cumulative Running Totals, Moving Averages.
- Common Table Expressions (CTEs): Non-recursive CTEs and Recursive CTEs for hierarchical tree structures.
- Date & Time manipulation: DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT, INTERVAL arithmetic, timezone handling.
- String & Regex functions: CONCAT, SUBSTRING, COALESCE, NULLIF, regex matching.

4) Phase 4 — Database Internals & Performance Tuning (Expert):
- Indexing Strategies: B-Tree, Hash, Composite Indexes, Covering Indexes (INCLUDE), Clustered vs Non-Clustered.
- Query Optimization: EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution plans, SARGable predicates, eliminating full table scans.
- Database Objects: Stored Procedures (SP), User-Defined Functions (UDF), Standard Views, Materialized Views, Triggers.
- Concurrency & Transactions: ACID properties, isolation levels (Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable), locking mechanisms.
- Database Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, denormalization tradeoffs.

title: Essential SQL Topics & Practice Checklist for Interviews & Projects
tags: topic of sql to start practice
content:
Top SQL topics to practice systematically for real-world mastery and technical interviews:

1) Filtering & Basic Retrieval:
- Filtering with multiple AND/OR logic, NOT IN with NULL caveats, wildcard search with LIKE '%abc%'.
- Handling NULL values properly with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL and COALESCE().

2) Relational Joins:
- Joining 3+ tables with foreign keys.
- Identifying missing records using LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL (Anti-Join).
- Many-to-many relationship queries using associative junction tables.

3) Aggregation & Group Filtering:
- Calculating metrics grouped by multiple columns.
- Filtering aggregated groups using HAVING (e.g. customers with total spend > $10,000).
- Conditional aggregation using SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).

4) Subqueries & Set Theory:
- Correlated subqueries: finding employees earning more than their department average.
- EXISTS vs IN performance on large datasets.
- Combining result sets using UNION vs UNION ALL.

5) Window Functions:
- Top N records per category using ROW_NUMBER() or DENSE_RANK() with PARTITION BY.
- Calculating Month-over-Month growth rate using (current_month - LAG(current_month, 1)) / LAG(current_month, 1).
- Running cumulative totals using SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING).

6) CTEs & Hierarchies:
- Refactoring complex nested subqueries into readable WITH clauses.
- Querying organizational manager-employee hierarchies using WITH RECURSIVE.

7) Schema Design & Optimization:
- Designing tables with PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY (ON DELETE CASCADE), UNIQUE, and CHECK constraints.
- Creating B-Tree indexes on filtered and joined columns.
- Analyzing EXPLAIN output to verify index usage.

title: SQL Interview Cheatsheet: Top 25 Rapid-Fire Architectural Concepts
content:
Quick architectural reference for technical SQL interviews:

1) Execution Order: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.
2) WHERE vs HAVING: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregated buckets.
3) UNION vs UNION ALL: UNION removes duplicates (slow sort); UNION ALL concatenates (fast).
4) DELETE vs TRUNCATE: DELETE is DML (logged per row, rollbackable); TRUNCATE is DDL (deallocates pages, resets identity).
5) Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index: Clustered determines physical table sort order (1 per table); Non-clustered is a secondary pointer tree.
6) SARGable: Avoid wrapping columns in functions inside WHERE (e.g. use `date >= '2025-01-01'` instead of `YEAR(date) = 2025`).
7) Stored Procedure vs Function: Procedure uses CALL, executes DML, manages transactions; Function uses SELECT, returns a value, no transactions.

title: SQL Beginner Guide: Relational Model, Tables, Rows, and Data Types
content:
An introduction to relational database systems for beginners:

1) Relational Database Concepts: Data is organized into structured two-dimensional tables (relations) comprising rows (records/tuples) and columns (attributes/fields).
2) Primary Key: Ensures every row has a unique identifier.
3) Foreign Key: Establishes connections between related tables (e.g. linking order records to customer records).
4) Declarative Nature: In SQL, you declare WHAT data you want, and the database query engine determines HOW to retrieve it efficiently.

title: Production SQL Performance Optimization Checklist
content:
10-point checklist for auditing and accelerating slow production SQL queries:

1) Eliminate SELECT * — Project only required columns to reduce memory buffer usage.
2) Check SARGability — Ensure WHERE predicates do not wrap indexed columns in functions.
3) Verify Index Usage — Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to ensure Index Seeks instead of Sequential Table Scans.
4) Avoid Redundant Sorting — Use UNION ALL instead of UNION when duplicates are impossible.
5) Replace Correlated Subqueries — Refactor into JOINs or CTEs with window functions where applicable.
6) Check Join Key Data Types — Mismatched join types prevent index usage (e.g. INT vs VARCHAR).
7) Filter Early — Apply WHERE filters before joining large intermediate tables.
8) Use Keyset Pagination — Replace deep `OFFSET 1000000` with `WHERE id > last_seen_id`.
9) Update Statistics — Ensure the Cost-Based Optimizer has fresh table statistics (`ANALYZE table`).
10) Add Covering Indexes — Use `INCLUDE` to create Index-Only Scans for high-frequency queries.

title: SELECT Statement: Projection, Mathematical Expressions, and Aliasing
content:
The SELECT statement specifies the column projections and scalar calculations returned by a query:

1) Column Projection: Project specific columns to reduce I/O.
2) Aliasing (AS): Rename columns or table references.
3) Expressions: Compute mathematical, string, or conditional expressions inline.

```sql
SELECT emp_id, first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name, salary * 1.10 AS next_year_salary FROM employees;
```

title: SELECT DISTINCT: Multi-Column Deduplication and Execution Cost
content:
SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows across all projected columns:

1) Multi-Column Scope: Uniqueness is evaluated across the combined tuple of all SELECT columns.
2) Cost: Incurs an implicit sorting or hashing step in memory/tempdb.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT department_id, job_title FROM employees;
```

title: WHERE Clause: Row-Level Filtering, Predicates, and Comparison Operators
content:
WHERE filters individual table records before grouping and aggregation:

1) Operators: `=`, `<>`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `BETWEEN`, `IN`, `LIKE`, `IS NULL`.
2) Logical Combining: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`.

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'COMPLETED' AND total_amount >= 500;
```

title: Boolean Logic: AND, OR, NOT Precedence and Parentheses Grouping
content:
Boolean operator precedence rules:

1) Hierarchy: `NOT` evaluates first, `AND` second, `OR` third.
2) Always use parentheses `()` to avoid logic bugs with mixed `AND` / `OR` conditions.

```sql
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE (account_type = 'PREMIUM' OR balance > 50000) AND is_active = TRUE;
```

title: IN and NOT IN Operators: List Membership and the NULL Trap
content:
IN tests if a value matches any element in a list or subquery:

1) NOT IN with NULLs: If the subquery contains ANY NULL, `NOT IN` returns 0 rows (evaluates to UNKNOWN). Use `NOT EXISTS` or filter `WHERE col IS NOT NULL`.

```sql
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL);
```

title: BETWEEN Operator: Inclusive Range Filtering on Numbers and Dates
content:
BETWEEN tests whether a value falls within an inclusive boundary ($low \le val \le high$):

1) Inclusivity: Both boundary values are included.
2) Timestamp Caution: For timestamps, use `>= '2025-01-01' AND < '2025-02-01'` to avoid missing partial days.

```sql
SELECT * FROM products WHERE unit_price BETWEEN 50 AND 200;
```

title: LIKE, ILIKE and Wildcards (%, _) with ESCAPE Sequences
content:
Text pattern matching:

1) `%`: Matches zero or more characters.
2) `_`: Matches exactly one character.
3) `ILIKE`: Case-insensitive matching (PostgreSQL).
4) Indexing: SARGable prefix search (`LIKE 'abc%'`) uses B-Tree indexes; leading wildcards (`LIKE '%abc'`) force full table scans.

```sql
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE email LIKE '%@company.com';
```

title: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL: Three-Valued Logic and Predicate Evaluation
content:
NULL represents missing or unknown information:

1) Rule: Never use `= NULL` or `!= NULL` (always evaluates to UNKNOWN). Use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.

```sql
SELECT emp_name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL;
```

title: ORDER BY Clause: Multi-Column Sorting, ASC/DESC, and NULLS FIRST/LAST
content:
ORDER BY sorts query result rows:

1) Direction: `ASC` (default) or `DESC`.
2) Multi-Column: Evaluated left-to-right.
3) NULL Ordering: Control NULL placement using `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST`.

```sql
SELECT emp_name, department_id, salary FROM employees ORDER BY department_id ASC, salary DESC NULLS LAST;
```

title: LIMIT and OFFSET: Pagination Mechanics and Keyset Pagination
content:
LIMIT and OFFSET paginate query rows:

1) Mechanics: `LIMIT n OFFSET m` skips `m` rows and returns `n` rows.
2) Keyset Optimization: Avoid deep `OFFSET 1000000` by filtering on indexed IDs: `WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT 10`.

```sql
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY product_id ASC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;
```

title: CASE WHEN: Searched CASE, Simple CASE, and Conditional Aggregation
content:
CASE WHEN provides conditional IF-THEN-ELSE evaluation:

1) Searched CASE: Evaluates boolean expressions in order.
2) Placement: Usable in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, and inside aggregates for pivoting.

```sql
SELECT emp_name, salary, CASE WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'Senior' ELSE 'Junior' END AS seniority_tier FROM employees;
```

title: COALESCE: Fallback Selection and Short-Circuiting
content:
COALESCE evaluates arguments left-to-right and returns the first non-NULL expression:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COALESCE(phone, mobile, email, 'No Contact') AS primary_contact FROM customers;
```

title: NULLIF: Preventing Division by Zero and Blank Value Handling
content:
NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL if a = b; otherwise returns a:

1) Division Safety: `total_cost / NULLIF(item_count, 0)` returns NULL instead of throwing a divide-by-zero exception.

```sql
SELECT dept_id, revenue / NULLIF(headcount, 0) AS revenue_per_head FROM departments;
```

title: CAST and CONVERT: Explicit Data Type Conversion Syntax
content:
Type conversion operators in SQL:

1) ANSI CAST: `CAST(val AS target_type)`.
2) PostgreSQL shorthand: `val::target_type`.
3) SQL Server: `CONVERT(target_type, val, [style])`.

```sql
SELECT CAST('2025-01-01' AS DATE), CAST(150.5 AS INT);
```

title: Logical SQL Query Processing & Execution Sequence
tags: what is execution order in sql
content:
The 8-step logical execution order of SQL queries:

1. FROM & JOIN
2. WHERE
3. GROUP BY
4. HAVING
5. SELECT
6. DISTINCT
7. ORDER BY
8. LIMIT / OFFSET

💡 Consequence: Aliases created in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE because WHERE executes in Step 2 before SELECT in Step 5.

title: INNER JOIN: Syntax, Equi-Joins, and Multi-Table Join Paths
content:
INNER JOIN returns rows where matching keys exist in both tables:

```sql
SELECT e.emp_name, d.dept_name FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
```

title: LEFT JOIN: Preserving Left Records, Outer Matches, and NULL Filters
content:
LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table with matched right rows (or NULL if unmatched):

```sql
SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

title: RIGHT JOIN: Preserving Right Records and Left Join Equivalence
content: RIGHT JOIN preserves all right table rows. `A RIGHT JOIN B` is equivalent to `B LEFT JOIN A`.

title: FULL OUTER JOIN: Complete Bidirectional Outer Joins
content:
FULL OUTER JOIN combines LEFT and RIGHT outer joins, returning all rows from both tables filled with NULLs where unmatched.

```sql
SELECT e.emp_name, d.dept_name FROM employees e FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
```

title: CROSS JOIN: Cartesian Products ($M \times N$) and Matrix Generation
content:
CROSS JOIN pairs every left row with every right row ($M \times N$ rows). Used for calendar matrices and permutations.

```sql
SELECT p.product_name, s.size_label FROM products p CROSS JOIN product_sizes s;
```

title: NATURAL JOIN: Implicit Join by Matching Column Names & Risks
content: NATURAL JOIN automatically joins tables on all columns sharing identical names. Incurring high maintenance risk if column names change; explicit `ON` clauses are strongly preferred in production.

title: SELF JOIN: Joining a Table to Itself for Hierarchies and Graph Edges
content:
SELF JOIN joins a table with itself using distinct aliases:

```sql
SELECT e.emp_name AS employee, m.emp_name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;
```

title: ANTI-JOIN: Finding Unmatched Rows via LEFT JOIN IS NULL and NOT EXISTS
content:
ANTI-JOIN returns left rows with NO matching right rows:

```sql
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL;
```

title: SEMI-JOIN: Existence Filtering via EXISTS without Multiplying Rows
content:
SEMI-JOIN checks existence in a secondary table without duplicating left rows:

```sql
SELECT * FROM departments d WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id);
```

title: LATERAL JOIN & CROSS APPLY: Correlated Table Expressions in FROM
content:
LATERAL (or CROSS APPLY) allows a subquery in FROM to reference preceding columns (for-each evaluation):

```sql
SELECT c.customer_id, o.total_amount FROM customers c CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT total_amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 1) o;
```

title: OUTER APPLY: Left Outer Correlated Subqueries in SQL Server / Oracle
content: OUTER APPLY functions like a LEFT JOIN to a correlated table expression, preserving outer rows even if the inner subquery returns 0 rows.

title: Non-Equi Joins: Range Joins, Inequality Joins, and Banding
content:
Non-equi joins join tables using `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, or `BETWEEN`:

```sql
SELECT e.emp_name, e.salary, g.grade_level FROM employees e JOIN salary_grades g ON e.salary BETWEEN g.min_salary AND g.max_salary;
```

title: Join Physical Algorithms: Nested Loops, Hash Join, and Merge Join
content:
Database physical join algorithms:

1) Nested Loops: Iterates outer rows and performs index seek on inner table. Best for small outer sets.
2) Hash Join: Builds hash table of smaller table in memory and scans larger table. Best for large unsorted sets.
3) Merge Join: Merges two pre-sorted inputs. Extremely fast when inputs are already sorted by join key.

title: SQL Set Operations: UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT
content:
Set operations combine rows from compatible SELECT queries:

1) UNION: Eliminates duplicates.
2) UNION ALL: Retains all duplicates with maximum speed.
3) INTERSECT: Returns common rows.
4) EXCEPT: Returns rows in query 1 not in query 2.

```sql
SELECT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT city FROM suppliers;
```

title: Set Operations Rules: Column Counts, Data Type Compatibility, and ORDER BY
content:
Rules for set operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT):

1) Identical Column Count: All queries must select the exact same number of columns.
2) Compatible Types: Corresponding columns must have compatible types in positional order.
3) Single ORDER BY: ORDER BY is placed once at the very end of the final query.

title: Aggregate Functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and NULL Handling
content: Aggregate functions summarize multiple values into a single scalar value. Note: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX automatically ignore NULL values; COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs.

title: GROUP BY Clause: Grouping Keys and Aggregation Semantics
content:
GROUP BY groups rows sharing identical grouping keys into summary records:

```sql
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
```

title: HAVING Clause: Post-Aggregation Group Filtering
content:
HAVING filters aggregated groups after GROUP BY:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total_amount) AS total_spent FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(total_amount) > 10000;
```

title: WHERE vs HAVING Clause: Execution Phase, Filtering Level, and Rules
content:
WHERE filters raw rows before aggregation; HAVING filters aggregated group metrics after aggregation.

```sql
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 75000;
```

title: COUNT(DISTINCT col): Counting Unique Non-Null Values
content: COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values in a column. Incurs hash table allocation or sorting in query execution.

title: ROLLUP: Hierarchical Subtotals and Grand Total Generation
content:
ROLLUP generates hierarchical subtotals and grand totals:

```sql
SELECT region, department_id, SUM(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, department_id);
```

title: CUBE: Multidimensional Aggregations Across All Dimension Permutations
content:
CUBE computes subtotals for all $2^N$ combinations of grouping columns:

```sql
SELECT region, category, SUM(sales) FROM sales_data GROUP BY CUBE (region, category);
```

title: GROUPING SETS: Custom Granular Multi-Level Grouping Combinations
content:
GROUPING SETS specifies explicit subtotal combinations in a single query pass without UNION ALL:

```sql
SELECT region, department_id, SUM(sales) FROM sales_data GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((region, department_id), (region), ());
```

title: STRING_AGG, GROUP_CONCAT, and LISTAGG: Delimited String Aggregation
content:
Concatenates text values across grouped rows into a delimited string:

```sql
-- PostgreSQL:
SELECT department_id, STRING_AGG(emp_name, ', ' ORDER BY salary DESC) AS team FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
```

title: ARRAY_AGG: Aggregating Column Values into Native SQL Arrays
content:
ARRAY_AGG collects grouped values into a native array (PostgreSQL / BigQuery):

```sql
SELECT department_id, ARRAY_AGG(emp_id ORDER BY hire_date) AS emp_ids FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
```

title: Conditional Aggregation: Pivoting Rows to Columns via SUM(CASE WHEN)
content:
Computes multiple category totals in a single table scan:

```sql
SELECT region, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'COMPLETED' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS completed_rev, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'REFUNDED' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS refund_rev FROM orders GROUP BY region;
```

title: PIVOT and UNPIVOT: Native Matrix Transposition Syntax
content: PIVOT rotates rows into columns; UNPIVOT rotates columns back into rows (supported natively in SQL Server and Oracle).

title: Statistical Aggregates: STDDEV_SAMP, VAR_SAMP, CORR, and MEDIAN
content: Standard statistical functions in SQL: `STDDEV_SAMP()` (sample standard deviation), `VAR_SAMP()` (sample variance), `CORR(y, x)` (Pearson correlation coefficient).

title: GROUPING() and GROUPING_ID(): Identifying Subtotal Rows
content: GROUPING(col) returns 1 if the row represents an aggregate subtotal generated by ROLLUP/CUBE, and 0 if it is a standard grouped row.

title: FILTER Clause on Aggregates: ANSI Standard Conditional Aggregation
content:
ANSI SQL standard FILTER clause (supported in PostgreSQL and SQLite 3.30+):

```sql
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE salary > 80000) AS high_earners FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
```

title: Anatomy of Window Functions: OVER, PARTITION BY, and ORDER BY
content:
Window functions perform calculations across a partition of rows related to the current row without collapsing rows:

`FUNCTION() OVER (PARTITION BY part_col ORDER BY sort_col [frame])`

```sql
SELECT emp_name, salary, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) AS dept_avg FROM employees;
```

title: ROW_NUMBER(): Sequential Row Indexing, Deduplication, and Top-N
content: Assigns a unique sequential integer (1, 2, 3, ...) per partition with no ties. Used for Top-N per group and deduplication.

title: RANK(): Ranking with Gaps on Tied Values
content: Assigns identical rank to ties, skipping subsequent numbers (1, 2, 2, 4).

title: DENSE_RANK(): Ranking Without Gaps on Tied Values
content: Assigns identical rank to ties without skipping subsequent numbers (1, 2, 2, 3).

title: RANK vs DENSE_RANK: Tie-Handling Differences and Leaderboards
content: RANK leaves gaps (1, 2, 2, 4); DENSE_RANK leaves no gaps (1, 2, 2, 3).

title: NTILE(n): Dividing Data into Quartiles, Deciles, and Percentiles
content:
NTILE(n) divides ordered rows into 'n' equal buckets (1 to n):

```sql
SELECT emp_name, salary, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS quartile FROM employees;
```

title: LAG(): Fetching Previous Row Values and Day-over-Day Growth
content:
LAG(col, offset, default) retrieves values from preceding rows:

```sql
SELECT order_date, revenue, LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_rev FROM daily_sales;
```

title: LEAD(): Fetching Subsequent Future Row Values and Churn Analysis
content: LEAD(col, offset, default) retrieves values from subsequent future rows.

title: FIRST_VALUE() and LAST_VALUE(): Partition Boundary Values
content: FIRST_VALUE(col) and LAST_VALUE(col) return the first or last value in the window frame.

title: NTH_VALUE(): Accessing Specific Row Positions in Window Partitions
content: NTH_VALUE(col, n) returns the value from the n-th row of the window frame.

title: CUME_DIST() and PERCENT_RANK(): Cumulative Distribution & Percentiles
content: CUME_DIST() computes the relative rank of a value ($row\_num / total\_rows$); PERCENT_RANK() computes relative percentage ($(rank - 1) / (total - 1)$).

title: ROWS vs RANGE BETWEEN: Physical Row Frames vs Logical Value Frames
content: ROWS defines frames by physical row count; RANGE defines frames by logical value intervals based on ORDER BY.

title: Cumulative Running Totals: Syntax and Execution Efficiency
content: Calculates cumulative totals using `SUM(col) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.

title: Rolling Moving Averages: 7-Day, 30-Day, and Centered Moving Averages
content: Calculates moving averages: `AVG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.

title: Aggregate Window Functions: SUM(), AVG(), COUNT() with OVER()
content: Using standard aggregate functions with `OVER()` computes partition summaries without collapsing row details.

title: Common Table Expressions (CTEs): WITH Clause, Modularity, and Readability
content:
A CTE defines a temporary named result set within a single SQL statement using `WITH`:

```sql
WITH HighEarners AS (SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 80000) SELECT * FROM HighEarners;
```

title: WITH RECURSIVE: Tree Hierarchies, Anchor/Recursive Members, and Graphs
content:
Recursive CTEs iterate over parent-child hierarchies using an Anchor Member, UNION ALL, and a Recursive Member.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE Tree AS (SELECT id, parent_id, 1 AS level FROM nodes WHERE parent_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT n.id, n.parent_id, t.level + 1 FROM nodes n JOIN Tree t ON n.parent_id = t.id) SELECT * FROM Tree;
```

title: Chained Multiple CTEs: Multi-Stage Data Transformation Pipelines
content:
Multiple CTEs can be defined in a single WITH statement separated by commas:

```sql
WITH Step1 AS (SELECT ...), Step2 AS (SELECT ... FROM Step1) SELECT * FROM Step2;
```

title: CTE vs Subquery vs Temporary Table vs View Comparison
content: CTEs enhance statement readability; Subqueries evaluate inline; Temp Tables persist intermediate data across statements; Views permanently store query definitions.

title: Deduplicating Data with CTEs and ROW_NUMBER()
content:
Identify duplicate records using a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() and delete where `row_num > 1`.

```sql
WITH Ranked AS (SELECT ctid, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY created_at DESC) as r FROM users) DELETE FROM users WHERE ctid IN (SELECT ctid FROM Ranked WHERE r > 1);
```

title: Data-Modifying CTEs: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE with RETURNING in CTEs
content: PostgreSQL allows DML statements with `RETURNING` inside CTEs, moving deleted/inserted rows into audit tables in a single atomic transaction.

title: MATERIALIZED vs NOT MATERIALIZED CTEs (PostgreSQL 12+ Optimization)
content: PostgreSQL 12+ automatically inlines CTEs unless specified as `WITH cte AS MATERIALIZED (...)` to force a materialization fence.

title: Graph Path Finding & Cycle Detection in Recursive CTEs
content: Track visited node arrays (`ARRAY[id]`) in recursive CTEs to prevent infinite loops in cyclic graphs.

title: Windowed Pagination and Total Count in a Single CTE Query
content: Compute total row count and paginated rows in a single query pass using CTEs with `COUNT(*) OVER()`.

title: CTE Performance Pitfalls: Optimization Fences and TempDB Overhead
content: Older database versions treat CTEs as strict optimization fences, preventing predicate pushdown. Verify query plans.

title: Scalar Subqueries: Single-Value Subqueries in SELECT and WHERE
content: A scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column. If it returns 0 rows, it evaluates to NULL; if >1 row, it throws a runtime error.

title: Multi-Row Subqueries: IN, ANY, ALL, and SOME Operators
content: Multi-row subqueries return a single column with multiple rows for evaluation with `IN`, `ANY` (true if any match), and `ALL` (true only if all match).

title: Correlated Subqueries: Row-by-Row Outer References
content:
Correlated subqueries reference outer query columns and evaluate once per candidate row.

```sql
SELECT * FROM employees e1 WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e1.dept_id);
```

title: EXISTS vs IN: Short-Circuiting, Subquery Optimization, and Performance
content: EXISTS terminates on the first match (short-circuiting); IN materializes the entire set into memory.

title: NOT EXISTS vs NOT IN: The NULL Hazard and Performance Differences
content: NOT IN fails if the subquery returns any NULL; NOT EXISTS is completely immune to NULL hazards and executes faster.

title: Derived Tables: Inline Subqueries in FROM Clauses and Mandatory Aliasing
content: A subquery placed in the FROM clause acts as a temporary in-memory table. In standard SQL, derived tables MUST have an explicit alias.

title: ANY, SOME, and ALL Operators in Subquery Comparisons
content: `> ANY (subquery)` is true if greater than the minimum value; `> ALL (subquery)` is true only if greater than the maximum value.

title: Subqueries in SELECT List: Column-Level Lookup Patterns
content:
Evaluate lookup metrics per row without explicit joins:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, (SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS latest_order FROM customers c;
```

title: Subqueries in HAVING Clauses: Dynamic Aggregate Thresholds
content:
Compare group aggregates against dynamic thresholds:

```sql
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING AVG(salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);
```

title: Subqueries in DML: INSERT INTO SELECT, UPDATE with Subqueries, DELETE Subqueries
content: Using subqueries to drive bulk inserts, updates, and deletes across relational tables.

title: Subquery Unnesting & Decorrelation in Modern Query Optimizers
content: Modern query optimizers automatically transform correlated subqueries into semi-joins or hash joins to avoid nested loops.

title: Inline Views vs CTEs: Readability and Scope
content: Inline views define temporary tables in FROM; CTEs provide equivalent capability with top-down readability.

title: Primary Key (PK): Definition, Characteristics, and Entity Integrity
content: A Primary Key uniquely identifies each row (Unique + NOT NULL, 1 per table, clustered index by default).

title: Foreign Key (FK): Definition, Referential Integrity, and Cascade Actions
content: A Foreign Key enforces Referential Integrity between child and parent tables (`ON DELETE CASCADE / RESTRICT / SET NULL`).

title: Primary Key vs Foreign Key: Entity Integrity vs Referential Integrity
tags: difference between primary and foreign key
what us difference between primary and foreign key
content: Primary Key guarantees row uniqueness within a table; Foreign Key guarantees data consistency across related tables.

title: CHECK Constraints: Domain Validation and Multi-Column Rules
content:
CHECK constraints validate column values on INSERT/UPDATE:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD CONSTRAINT check_positive_price CHECK (unit_price > 0);
```

title: UNIQUE Constraint: Uniqueness Enforcement, Indexes, and NULLs
content: UNIQUE ensures column values are distinct. Unlike PKs, multiple UNIQUE constraints can exist per table, and NULLs are allowed.

title: NOT NULL Constraint: Enforcing Mandatory Field Values
content: NOT NULL prevents missing or unassigned values from being stored in a column.

title: DEFAULT Constraint: Automatic Column Value Insertion
content:
DEFAULT supplies an initial value when no value is specified in an INSERT statement:

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN status SET DEFAULT 'PENDING';
```

title: AUTO_INCREMENT, SERIAL, IDENTITY, and SEQUENCES
content: System-generated surrogate primary keys: `AUTO_INCREMENT` (MySQL), `SERIAL` / `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` (PostgreSQL), `IDENTITY(1,1)` (SQL Server), `SEQUENCE.NEXTVAL` (Oracle).

title: ALTER TABLE: Adding, Dropping, Renaming Columns and Constraints
content:
DDL command for schema evolution:

```sql
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20), DROP COLUMN fax_number;
```

title: DROP TABLE vs TRUNCATE TABLE: Complete Destruction vs Bulk Data Purge
content: DROP TABLE destroys the table structure, metadata, constraints, and data; TRUNCATE preserves schema structure and empties data pages instantly.

title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP: Logging, Rollbacks, and Resets
tags: what is the difference between delete, truncate and drop
content: DELETE is DML (row logged, rollbackable, fires triggers); TRUNCATE is DDL (page deallocated, fast, resets identity); DROP is DDL (destroys table structure).

title: Database Schemas & Namespaces: Organizing Tables & Security
content: Schemas organize database objects into distinct logical namespaces (`sales.orders`, `hr.employees`) for multi-tenant isolation and security permissions.

title: Temporary Tables: Local (#temp), Global (##temp), and pg_temp
content: Temporary tables persist data only during the current session or transaction, supporting custom indexes for heavy intermediate computations.

title: Table Partitioning: Range, List, Hash Partitioning & Pruning
content: Partition massive tables into physically separate chunks based on date ranges, regions, or hash buckets, enabling Partition Pruning during queries.

title: Cascading Referential Actions: CASCADE, RESTRICT, SET NULL
content:
Define what happens to child records when parent records are deleted or updated:

```sql
FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE ON UPDATE CASCADE
```

title: INSERT Statement: Single-Row, Multi-Row, and Default Value Inserts
content:
Insert new records into tables:

```sql
INSERT INTO products (product_name, unit_price) VALUES ('Widget A', 19.99), ('Widget B', 29.99);
```

title: INSERT INTO SELECT: Bulk Data Migration and Table Population
content:
Populates a table directly from query results:

```sql
INSERT INTO archive_orders SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date < '2024-01-01';
```

title: UPDATE Statement: Modifying Rows, WHERE Safeguards, and Calculated Updates
content:
Modifies existing records. Always include a WHERE clause to prevent updating all rows across the entire table!

```sql
UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.05 WHERE department_id = 10;
```

title: UPDATE with JOIN: Cross-Table Updates across Relational Datasets
content:
Update columns based on joined tables:

```sql
-- PostgreSQL / SQLite UPDATE FROM:
UPDATE products p SET unit_price = p.unit_price * 1.1 FROM suppliers s WHERE p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id AND s.region = 'EMEA';
```

title: DELETE Statement: Removing Specific Rows and Transaction Safeguards
content: Removes records matching WHERE criteria. Logs individual row deletions in transaction logs, enabling ROLLBACK.

title: DELETE with JOIN: Removing Child Records Based on Parent Joins
content: Delete records based on relational join filters (e.g. `DELETE FROM orders USING customers WHERE ...`).

title: UPSERT & MERGE: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
content: Conditional insert/update syntax: `ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE` in PostgreSQL/SQLite; `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` in MySQL; `MERGE` in SQL Server/Oracle.

title: RETURNING and OUTPUT: Returning Modified Rows Directly from DML
content:
Returns newly generated keys or updated data immediately without extra SELECT queries:

```sql
INSERT INTO users (username) VALUES ('alice') RETURNING user_id, created_at;
```

title: Bulk Data Loading: COPY FROM, BULK INSERT, and LOAD DATA INFILE
content: High-speed binary and CSV ingestion methods bypassing standard statement parsing overhead.

title: SELECT INTO: Creating and Populating New Tables in One Step
content: Create and populate a new table from query results (`SELECT INTO new_table FROM old_table` or `CREATE TABLE new_table AS SELECT ...`).

title: ACID Properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
content: Relational transaction guarantees: Atomicity (All or nothing), Consistency (Preserves constraints), Isolation (No concurrent corruption), Durability (Persisted to disk/WAL).

title: SQL Isolation Levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable
content:
Transaction isolation levels from lowest to highest strictness:

1) Read Uncommitted (Allows dirty reads)
2) Read Committed (Default in Postgres/Oracle)
3) Repeatable Read (Default in MySQL InnoDB)
4) Serializable (Strictest, full isolation)

title: Dirty Reads: Reading Uncommitted Data in Concurrency
content: A Dirty Read occurs when Transaction A reads data modified by Transaction B that has NOT yet been committed (and could be rolled back).

title: Non-Repeatable Reads: Value Changes Between Consecutive Queries
content: A Non-Repeatable Read occurs when Transaction A reads a row, Transaction B updates that row and commits, and Transaction A re-reads the row to find changed values.

title: Phantom Reads: New Row Insertions in Range Queries
content: A Phantom Read occurs when Transaction A queries a range of rows (e.g. `salary > 50000`), Transaction B inserts a new matching row and commits, and Transaction A re-runs the query to find new 'phantom' rows.

title: Database Locks: Shared (S) vs Exclusive (X) and Lock Granularity
content: Shared (S) locks allow concurrent readers; Exclusive (X) locks give sole write access, blocking all other readers and writers.

title: Deadlocks: Detection, Victim Selection, and Prevention Strategies
content: A Deadlock occurs when two transactions wait for locks held by each other. Databases detect cycles and abort one transaction as the 'victim'. Prevent by acquiring locks in consistent order.

title: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) Internals
content: MVCC ensures Readers do not block Writers, and Writers do not block Readers by maintaining row version timestamps (xmin/xmax).

title: TCL Commands: BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
content: Explicit transaction management commands to guarantee atomicity and partial rollback points (`SAVEPOINT sp1`).

title: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and Durability Architecture
content: WAL writes transaction changes sequentially to an append-only log on disk BEFORE modifying table data pages, ensuring instant crash recovery.

title: Pessimistic Locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) vs Optimistic Locking (Version Check)
content: Pessimistic locking locks rows explicitly (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`); Optimistic locking checks version numbers upon update without holding locks.

title: Two-Phase Commit (2PC): Distributed Transaction Coordination
content: Coordinates atomic transactions across multiple distinct physical databases using Prepare and Commit phases.

title: B-Tree Index Architecture: Balanced Tree Traversal and Range Lookups
content: B-Tree indexes maintain sorted balanced tree structures supporting O(log N) lookups for equality and ranges (`=, <, >, BETWEEN, LIKE 'abc%'`).

title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Indexes: Physical Storage and Pointers
content: A Clustered Index determines the physical sort order of rows on disk (1 per table, typically PK). Non-Clustered indexes are secondary trees holding row pointers.

title: Composite Multi-Column Indexes and the Leftmost Prefix Rule
content: An index on `(A, B, C)` can serve queries filtering on `(A)`, `(A, B)`, or `(A, B, C)`, but CANNOT serve queries filtering on `(B)` or `(C)` alone.

title: Covering Indexes: The INCLUDE Clause and Index-Only Scans
content:
Covering indexes store extra columns in leaf pages via `INCLUDE`, fulfilling queries entirely from the index without reading table pages:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_cust ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (order_date, total_amount);
```

title: Filtered and Partial Indexes: Indexing Specific Table Subsets
content:
Index only rows matching a WHERE predicate to save disk space:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_active_orders ON orders (customer_id) WHERE status = 'PENDING';
```

title: Expression & Function-Based Indexes: Indexing Computed Columns
content:
Index computed expressions to accelerate non-SARGable queries:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_lower_email ON users (LOWER(email));
```

title: Index Seek vs Index Scan vs Sequential Table Scan Comparison
content: Index Seek navigates directly to matching keys (O(log N)); Index Scan reads all leaf pages; Table Scan reads all raw data blocks.

title: SARGable Query Design: Writing Index-Friendly Predicates
tags: how does sargable query optimization work
content: Avoid wrapping indexed columns in functions in WHERE clauses. Use range bounds rather than `YEAR(date)` or `DATE(date)`.

title: EXPLAIN & EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Interpreting Query Cost and Memory Buffers
content: EXPLAIN shows estimated optimizer plans; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query to measure actual millisecond latency and buffer hits.

title: Column Pruning: Avoiding SELECT * and Reducing Disk I/O
content: Projecting only necessary columns reduces RAM cache consumption, network serialization, and enables Index-Only Scans.

title: Index Maintenance: Fragmentation, Page Splits, and REINDEX / REORGANIZE
content: Frequent inserts/updates cause index page fragmentation. Reorganize or rebuild fragmented indexes to restore sequential read performance.

title: Cost-Based Optimizer (CBO), Statistics, Histograms, and ANALYZE
content: The CBO relies on column histograms and data distribution statistics to estimate row cardinality and choose optimal join algorithms.

title: Stored Procedures (SP): Complete Architecture, Parameters, and Syntax
content: Precompiled procedural code modules executed with `CALL` supporting loops, conditionals, transaction control, and parameter modes (`IN`, `OUT`, `INOUT`).

title: User-Defined Functions (UDF): Scalar vs Table-Valued Functions (TVF)
content: Reusable computational routines called inside queries (`SELECT my_func(col)`). Must return a value; cannot manage transactions.

title: Standard Views: Virtual Table Abstractions and Security Encapsulation
content: A virtual saved query definition that does not store physical data on disk. Simplifies joins and provides column masking.

title: Materialized Views: Physical Caching and Refresh Strategies
content: Physically persists query results on disk as a table for ultra-fast analytical reads. Requires explicit refresh (`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`).

title: Database Triggers: BEFORE, AFTER, INSTEAD OF, and Audit Logging
content: Event-driven procedures executed automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, with access to `OLD` and `NEW` records.

title: Updatable Views and the WITH CHECK OPTION Clause
content: Single-table views without aggregates can accept INSERT/UPDATE. `WITH CHECK OPTION` enforces that modified rows satisfy the view WHERE filter.

title: Database Cursors: Row-by-Row Iteration, Fetching, and Performance Caveats
content: Cursors iterate row-by-row through result sets. Slow in relational databases; set-based SQL operations should always be preferred.

title: Dynamic SQL: EXECUTE, sp_executesql, and SQL Injection Defenses
content: Constructing SQL strings dynamically at runtime. Always use parameterized execution (`sp_executesql` / `EXECUTE ... USING`) to prevent SQL injection.

title: Database Packages and Modules: Grouping Procedures & Functions in Oracle / DB2
content: Oracle PL/SQL packages encapsulate related procedures, functions, types, and variables into a single schema object.

title: LIMIT vs TOP vs FETCH FIRST: Syntax and Dialect Differences
content: Row limiting syntax: `LIMIT n` in PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQLite; `TOP (n)` in SQL Server; `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` in ANSI/Oracle.

title: Indexed Views (SQL Server) & Schema Binding
content: SQL Server allows creating a Clustered Index directly on a view with `WITH SCHEMABINDING`, physically persisting view data on disk.

title: Error Handling in Stored Procedures: TRY-CATCH and EXCEPTION Blocks
content: Structured exception handling inside procedures to catch errors and safely execute `ROLLBACK`.

title: Building Automated Audit Trail Tables with Triggers
content: Using AFTER UPDATE/DELETE triggers to insert previous values (`OLD.*`) and timestamps into dedicated audit tables.

title: Deterministic vs Non-Deterministic Functions in Query Optimization
content: Deterministic functions always return the same result for identical inputs, allowing the optimizer to cache results or build functional indexes.

title: Table-Valued Functions (TVF): Inline vs Multi-Statement TVFs
content: Functions returning a table result set that can be joined in FROM clauses like a parameterized view.

title: Numeric Data Types: INT, BIGINT, DECIMAL vs FLOAT
content: `INT`/`BIGINT` for whole numbers; `DECIMAL(p,s)` for exact fixed-point financial currency; `FLOAT` for approximate scientific floating point.

title: String Types: CHAR vs VARCHAR vs TEXT vs NVARCHAR
content: `CHAR(n)` is fixed-width padded with spaces; `VARCHAR(n)` is variable length; `TEXT` is unbounded string; `NVARCHAR` stores UTF-16 Unicode.

title: Date & Time Types: DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP, and TIMESTAMPTZ
content: `DATE` stores calendar day; `TIME` stores time-of-day; `TIMESTAMP` stores date+time; `TIMESTAMPTZ` stores timezone offsets.

title: Date Functions: DATE_TRUNC, EXTRACT, DATEDIFF, and DATEADD
content: Manipulate dates: `DATE_TRUNC('month', dt)` truncates timestamp; `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM dt)` extracts integer parts; `dt + INTERVAL '7 days'` adds intervals.

title: String Functions: CONCAT, SUBSTRING, REPLACE, TRIM, and UPPER/LOWER
content: Core string manipulation functions: `CONCAT()`, `SUBSTRING(str, start, len)`, `REPLACE(str, from, to)`, `TRIM()`, `UPPER()`, `LOWER()`.

title: Regular Expressions: REGEXP_LIKE, SIMILAR TO, and Regex Functions
content: Regex search in SQL: `WHERE col ~ '^[A-Z]{3}-[0-9]{4}$'` (PostgreSQL) or `WHERE REGEXP_LIKE(col, pattern)` (MySQL/Oracle).

title: JSON & JSONB in SQL: Query Operators (->, ->>), Indexing, and Search
content: PostgreSQL JSONB binary format supports `->` (returns JSON), `->>` (returns text), and GIN indexing for fast nested key lookups.

title: JSON Aggregation: JSON_BUILD_OBJECT, JSON_AGG, and JSON_ARRAY
content: Serialize relational rows directly into nested JSON structures using `JSON_BUILD_OBJECT()` and `JSON_AGG()`.

title: UUID / GUID Generation: UUIDv4 vs Sequential UUIDv7 in Primary Keys
